newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UNHCR asks Tanzania to separate refugee leaders.
newsitem.headline: UNHCR asks Tanzania to separate refugee leaders.

text.p: The U.N. refugee agency, reeling from a crisis in east Zaire and facing another in Tanzania, urged Tanzania on Friday to separate extremists from hundreds of thousands of refugees they are herding away from Rwanda.
A top official of the U.N. refugee agency said some 300,000 Rwandan Hutus had fled camps in Ngara near Tanzania's border with Rwanda and asked Tanzania to redirect them towards Rwanda.

Speaking at a news conference, Augustine Mahiga, UNHCR coordinator for Africa's troubled Great Lakes region, added that the refugees had walked only some 30 km (18 miles) inland and that Tanzanian authorities were confident of intercepting them quickly.
"The priority at the moment for UNHCR is to stop this movement and to work with the Tanzanian government not to use force in returning the refugees back towards Rwanda," he said.
"We also urge the Tanzanian government to take appropriate measures for the separation of leaders and intimidators whom we're convinced organised this movement," said Mahiga, who is Tanzanian.
Last month Tanzania gave the 540,000 Hutu refugees on its soil, who fled Rwanda in fear of reprisal for the 1994 Hutu-led genocide of Tutsis, until the end of this month to go home.

The plan was agreed by UNHCR, which has seen its core protection mandate buried in the war-ravaged region amid the forced return home of more than 550,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees and another 50,000 Burundians from eastern Zaire since October.
The U.N. human rights office says hundreds of returnees in Burundi were massacred by the army dominated by minority Tutsis.
The Tanzania flight is yet another nightmare for aid agencies which have yet to find another half a million Rwandan Hutus lost in eastern Zaire, fleeing a Tutsi rebellion.
Mahiga said Tanzania had assured the UNHCR any operation to redirect the flow would primarily involve the police.

Tanzania has in the past repeatedly pledged to separate Hutu extremists from the refugees. But nothing came out of these promises and it is hard to see how thousands of reluctant Hutus could be diverted towards Rwanda without the use of force.
The UNHCR said the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, Sadako Ogata, was in contact with the Tanzanian leaders, and Mahiga said UNHCR had no choice but to cooperate with Tanzania.
"We had a choice of either procrastinating the movement or being on board with Tanzania's decision. It was absolutely important that we are with Tanzanians to get their cooperation."
"The Tanzanians are very optimistic that this can be done before they disperse into smaller groups," Mahiga said.
On Friday, Tanzanian troops and police set up a roadblock near another camp, at Lumasi, and turned back up to 50,000 refugees, a U.N. World Food Programme official said.

Mahiga said mainly vulnerable people were left behind in the vast camps in Benaco, which was in effect Tanzania's second biggest city with refugee schools, hotels, mud brick houses with gardens, restaurants and thousands of hectares of farmland.
In Karagwe to the north, the movement had stopped and some 100,000 refugees remained out of 130,000, Mahiga said.

UNHCR has reported that the refugees said they were heading for Kenya and Malawi, but Mahiga doubted they could make it. Ngara is about 600 km (370 miles) west of the Kenyan border and 850 km (530 miles) northwest of the Malawi border.
